title: Fats & Oils
subtitle: 1000–1500 · Lent, Butter and the Oil Line: Basque Whalers, Tunisian Oil in the Geniza, the Song Oil Press and the Butter Tower of Rouen

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Lenten bans on butter, butter dispensations and royal taxes on whales

entries.label: Kings tax the whale: Biarritz 1197, Bayonne 1261, the royal fish 1324
entries.hint: In 1197 King John of England, as Duke of Guienne, taxed the first two whales taken at Biarritz; in 1261 every whale taken at Bayonne was tithed, continuing an older voluntary gift of whales’ tongues to the Church; and under a statute of 1324 known as De Praerogativa Regis Edward II claimed a duty on every whale captured in British waters, the ‘royal fish’. The kings of Castile and Navarre also took shares of whalers’ meat or whalebone.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis, Men and Whales (1991) p.45 (PDF p.68), drawing on Markham (1881) and Aguilar. The 1324 statute is Ellis’s; the legal wording and the reading of ‘royal fish’ were not checked.

entries.label: The Council of Angers forbids butter in Lent
entries.hint: French monks abstained from meat, lard and tallow but cooked their vegetables with butter or milk until this was emphatically restricted in 1365. The Council of Angers, as Le Grand d’Aussy reports it, knew that clerics in several regions used milk and butter in Lent even though they had fish and oil, and forbade them in bread and vegetables too unless permission had been granted. The offender risked a fine, prison or the whip.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; Le Grand d’Aussy not read): Khosrova, Butter: A Rich History (2016) pp.54–55 (PDF pp.75–76). The date 1365 is Khosrova’s for the restriction; she does not date the Angers canon separately, so the council may not be the 1365 act. Compare Flandrin, L’ordre des mets (on Lent excluding butter as well as lard).

entries.label: Anne of Brittany wins a butter dispensation
entries.hint: In 1491 Queen Anne, Duchess of Brittany, lobbied Rome for leave to use butter in Lent for her household, since Brittany produced no cooking oil and imported none; the whole of Brittany received the same allowance. By 1495 butter permission was granted to Germany, Hungary, Bohemia and France too, on condition of prayers and alms to the church. In the 13th century a butter allowance cost six deniers, the price of fifteen pounds of salt or a fat capon.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history): Khosrova (2016) pp.54–56 (PDF pp.76–77), who cites Bridget Henisch, Fast and Feast, for Luther’s remark of 1520. Her chain of grants (Brittany 1491, then 1495 elsewhere) was not checked against papal records.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The fasting calendar and the Butter Tower

entries.label: Half the year without butter: Lent and the oil line
entries.hint: By the early Middle Ages Christians fasted on Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays, on the eve of feasts, in part of Advent and for the forty days of Lent: roughly half the year. The rule bore very differently in the south, where olive oil, fish and grain carried on, and in the north, where the ban on milk, meat, cheese, butter and eggs was a forced starvation and a duty to eat imported oil was ‘as hard to digest as the foreign debts’. Medieval Provençal and Spanish travellers carried their own oil north, believing butter made one susceptible to leprosy, and unscrupulous Italian and Spanish merchants sent the worst oil north.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history): Khosrova (2016) pp.54–55 (PDF pp.75–76) on the fasting calendar and the north–south split, ‘it’s worth noting’ for the leprosy belief. Flandrin, L’ordre des mets, says Westerners abstained in Lent not only from lard and other animal fats but from butter, which distinguished Lent from ordinary Friday and Saturday abstinence; northern ‘butter eaters’ disliked oil, and he believes repugnance for oil cookery helped drive northern Europe toward the Reformation.

entries.label: The Butter Tower of Rouen
entries.hint: A 260-foot tower of Rouen cathedral, added between 1485 and 1507, is known as the Tour de Beurre; it is said to have been paid for by Catholics who bought the right to eat butter in Lent and on other fast days. In parts of France and Flanders churches put out troncs pour le beurre, alms boxes for butter. No accounts survive to show how much the dispensations actually paid for.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; tradition): Khosrova (2016) p.56 (PDF p.77) — ‘reportedly using the money’; ‘no accounting records exist to prove’ it. Treat the financing as a tradition, the dates as the tower’s.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Arab dishes in a Latin cookbook

entries.label: Arab dishes reach Latin cookbooks, with bacon fat for tail fat
entries.hint: Some Baghdad-style dishes reached the tables of the affluent in Christian Europe in name and technique, with changes such as bacon fat in place of sheep’s tail fat; the earliest mention of such dishes, on Rodinson’s reading, is in the Latin Liber de coquina of the late 13th century.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly introduction): Nasrallah, Annals of the Caliphs’ Kitchens (2007), Introduction (PDF p.41), citing Maxime Rodinson’s articles on Liber de coquina; the date is Nasrallah’s ‘towards the end of the thirteenth century’ as I read it, and was not checked against Rodinson.

entries.label: The court physician’s dietetics of 1330: sheep’s tail fat in the recipes
entries.hint: The Yinshan zhengyao, “Essentials of Dietetics”, presented to the Emperor by the court physician in 1330, makes heavy use of the tail fat of the fat-tailed sheep, both the mass itself and the rendered fat. Anderson notes that this fat has a flavour stronger but pleasanter than lard and is probably the most beloved food item throughout Central Asia, that nothing could be further from Chinese taste, and that the emphasis shows the book’s Mongol origin and audience; other recipes are Arabo-Persian or Turkic. Boiled mutton was probably the most important food after grains.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Anderson, The Food of China (1988), the Yuan section, PDF p.86 (citing Sukhov’s and Inalcık’s works there). Compare fats-600-1000::e1 for the same tail fat in the Baghdad cookbook and e1 here for the Arab dishes that reach Latin cookbooks.

entries.label: The Chi le pien: sesame best, and a dozen other oils
entries.hint: The Song miscellany Chi le pien (about 1190) says oil is used everywhere for eating and burning, the best coming from sesame (‘fragrant hemp’), and lists hemp oil for rain-garments, almond, hibiscus and rape-turnip oils in Shaanxi, cocklebur oil in Shandong, thick and filthy tung oil for lamps, a fragrant tree-seed oil for torches, fish oil in Yingzhou, and the hard oil of the Chinese tallow tree poured to form candles in Guangnan. The statesman Zu Ting is said to have lost his sight to rape-turnip smoke.
entries.note: SECONDARY (translation read in Needham): Needham, SCC 6.5 (2000) pp.440–441 (PDF pp.468–469), translating Chi le pien vol.1 p.25a via Mark Elvin (Shiba Yoshinobu 1970). Shen Kua (Meng chhi pi than) is cited there for the northern habit of frying in hemp oil.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Basque whaling, Tunisian oil in Egypt, Egyptian linseed, Hangzhou’s oil trade, palm oil on sale

entries.label: Polynesians settle Hawai‘i and New Zealand with their tree crops, AD 940–1280
entries.hint: Kirch dates the settlement of the Hawaiian Islands to between AD 940 and 1130, from the bones of the Pacific rat and from Polynesian-introduced plants such as candlenut, and the settlement of New Zealand, the last of the large islands to be colonised, to about AD 1280, from rat bones, with rat-gnawed seeds dated to AD 1140–1340. Candlenut is among the Polynesian-introduced plants carried by the voyagers; the passages say nothing about oil from it.
entries.note: CONTEXT (book read): Kirch, On the Road of the Winds (rev. ed.), ch.7, PDF p.222, citing Athens, Reith & Dye 2014 and Wilmshurst et al. 2008. The candlenut appears there as dating evidence, not as a fat; the fat reading is the folio’s, from Kirch’s coconut and nut-crop passages.

entries.label: The Basques hunt the right whale and sell its fat on fast days
entries.hint: The Basques are the first people known to hunt large whales in an organised way, apparently from about AD 1000 (Aguilar found a Bayonne reference of 1059), taking the right whale from watchtowers (vigías) along the Cantabrian coast. Blubber was sold as lard de carême, ‘Lenten fat’, which Europeans could eat on meatless days, and the oil lit lamps and went into soap, wool, leather and paint; the Basques kept ‘consulates’ in Holland, Denmark and England for sales. A San Sebastián petition of 1150 names whalebone among its goods.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis, Men and Whales (1991) pp.41–45 (PDF pp.65–68), citing Aguilar (the 1059 Bayonne record), Markham (1881; the 1150 Navarre grant), Ommanney (tenth-century origin from Norse whalers) and De Smet. Ellis says the Basque origin is lost and that Norse whaling may have come first (see fats-600-1000::ec5).

entries.label: Egypt’s flax, linseed oil and sesame
entries.hint: Next to wheat the common people’s nutrition depended mainly on oil. In Fatimid and Ayyubid Egypt, because of the enormous extent of flax growing, linseed oil was widely used, above all for lighting, and was exported from Egypt to olive-growing Syria and far-off Aden; sesame was grown in the northern Delta and in Palestine, and ‘maker of sesame oil’ is a frequent occupation. Oil and wax were the almost exclusive materials for artificial lighting. Safflower seed gave a medicinal oil.
entries.note: ANCHOR (translated documents read): Goitein (1967) vol.1 p.120 (PDF p.156; the Geniza records, 11th–13th centuries) and p.151 (PDF p.187) for the retail partnership of January 1104 with jars of linseed oil. Span as for the Geniza documents; individual dates not given in the passage.

entries.label: Thule hunters, bowhead whales and the oil lamp across the Arctic
entries.hint: The Thule people, who spread from Alaska across nearly the whole North American Arctic, relied for their winter stores largely on bowhead whales, and burned seal and whale oil in soapstone lamps that lit, heated and cooked in their winter houses. The old story tied the eastward spread to a warm spell that let the bowhead and its hunters move east; later critics doubt the eleventh-century dates, put the movement in the 1200s, and argue that whaling’s role at some sites may have been overstated. No European whale-oil trade lies behind any of this: it is a household fat economy.
entries.note: CONTESTED (dates and the role of whaling) / SECONDARY (museum and encyclopedia pages found by web search, not read in full): University of Alaska Museum, ‘Thule Culture’; Heritage Newfoundland and Labrador, ‘Thule’; a Historical Climatology article on McGhee’s revised dates; Schledermann 1981 as quoted on a secondary web page. The Thule tradition is dated roughly AD 1–1500; the qulliq lamp itself is far older, found at Norton-tradition sites.

entries.label: Tunisian oil for Egypt: five thousand skins in one season
entries.hint: Olive oil was almost absent from Egypt, yet a vital part of daily food and the choicest lighting oil, so its import was one of the great branches of Mediterranean trade; around 1065, in a famine, a merchant at Alexandria estimated the oil imported from Tunisia at five thousand skins, and eight days later at six thousand. Olive oil, soap and wax were among the Tunisian goods on the ledgers of the Geniza merchants, and ‘zayyāt’, oil-maker or seller, is among the commonest occupational names; some dealt in linseed oil, others were great importers of Tunisian oil.
entries.note: ANCHOR (translated documents read): Goitein, A Mediterranean Society vol.1 (1967) p.120 (PDF p.156; 1074 document, a press operator in 1203), p.154 (PDF p.190), p.215 (PDF p.251; the 5,000–6,000 skins of c.1065) and p.152 (PDF p.188) (OCR of a scanned PDF). The two estimates by the same merchant differ by a thousand skins, which Goitein reads as a sign of how rough such estimates were.

entries.label: Synagogue lamp oil in Fustat: monthly accounts of olive and linseed oil
entries.hint: Goitein notes that the monthly accounts of the Fustat synagogues’ expenditure on olive and linseed oil are extremely common in the Geniza and could be used with profit by anyone studying the history of lighting. Detailed lists of the lighting appliances survive from 1075 and 1080, soon after the great sack of the Egyptian capital by Turkish mercenaries, when even the caliph’s palaces were plundered.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Goitein, A Mediterranean Society vol. II: The Community (1971), the section on synagogue furnishings, PDF p.172. The accounts themselves are not read; this is Goitein’s description of them.

entries.label: Butter turns from a sheep’s luxury into an everyday cattle fat
entries.hint: In the High Middle Ages, as wool and milk became separate enterprises, dairy systems in England shifted from sheep to cattle, which made butter more affordable. Before long, Khosrova says, butter was so popular among all classes that making it was more profitable than making cheese.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; no source in the passage): Khosrova (2016) p.36 (PDF p.57). The span is her ‘high Middle Ages’; the claim that butter overtook cheese in profit is not dated or sourced there.

entries.label: Oil as money: three to five litres for a fat hog
entries.hint: Olive oil commanded a premium in the high Middle Ages and was often used as an alternative currency: in contracts, three to five litres of oil had the same value as a fat hog. Church councils protected olive groves because monks and priests needed oil for holy oils and church lamps.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; no contract cited): Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011), the passage after ‘In the sea of barbarian beer, butter, and lard’. The ‘high medieval contracts’ are not named, so the date is the folio’s span for the high Middle Ages.

entries.label: Oil among the seven necessities of Hangzhou
entries.hint: A Yuan-era account of the Southern Song capital Hangzhou says that the things people cannot do without each day are firewood, rice, oil, salt, soy paste, vinegar and tea; oil pressing establishments were seen in the city. By the Sung, Needham concludes, vegetable oil had become a major commodity, manufactured and traded throughout the land, whereas in the Zhou its place had been taken by animal fat.
entries.note: SECONDARY (translation read in Needham): Needham, SCC 6.5 (2000) pp.436–437 and 441 (PDF pp.464–465, 469), citing Meng liang lu ch.16 p.139 and ch.13 p.105 (Needham dates it 1334; the book describes the Southern Song capital, so the entry is dated by what it describes). Compare fats-1200bc-300bc::th2 for the Zhou fats.

entries.label: China’s su turns from butter into animal-fat shortening
entries.hint: The Yuan household encyclopaedia Ju jia bi yong includes sheep tallow or lard among the ingredients of its recipe for su, the butter-like fat of earlier centuries, which suggests that after the Yuan the word su no longer meant pure butter but simply a shortening based on animal fat; a reader of later recipes cannot assume that su is butter.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly note): Needham, SCC 6.5 (2000) p.254 (PDF p.282, n.90, citing Chü chia pi yung). Date of the Yuan work is given as ‘of the Yuan’; c.1300 is a placeholder for the dynasty. Chang (ed.), Food in Chinese Culture (1977), the Yüan and Ming chapter, PDF p.262 note 6, warns that su yu has long meant any animal fat, particularly mutton and beef tallow, so that it should not be read as butter wherever it appears in Ming texts (against Wada 1957), though imperial dairy herds still supplied butter for pastries at the end of the dynasty.

entries.label: Four Shanghai jars of coconut oil from Surabaya: a Banjarmasin chronicle
entries.loc: Surabaya and Banjarmasin, Java and Borneo
entries.hint: Reid cites the Banjarmasin chronicle, in which a hero of the fourteenth or fifteenth century comes back to Borneo from Surabaya with a thousand cakes of sugar, a hundred coconuts and four Shanghai jars of coconut oil, with tamarind, garlic, onions and rice: coconut oil is a good in the island trade in foodstuffs, and travels in Chinese jars.
entries.note: SECONDARY (book read; a chronicle episode, not a customs record): Reid, Southeast Asia in the Age of Commerce 1450–1680, vol.1 (1988) p.31 (PDF p.50), citing Hikayat Banjar pp.362–63. The date is the chronicle’s ‘fourteenth- or fifteenth-century’ hero.

entries.label: Palm oil on sale in West Africa: Cadamosto, then Pacheco Pereira
entries.loc: Senegal, the Forcados River and Benin
entries.hint: Cadamosto, writing in the 1460s, gives the first literary reference to palm oil in European sources: palm wine drunk and palm oil used in cooking in the Senegal region. Pacheco Pereira, who visited West Africa in the 1480s, records palm oil offered for sale along the Forcados River and says it was sold to European traders from at least the 1480s. Archaeology suggests West Africans cooked with palm oil 5,000 to 6,000 years ago, and Egyptians traded it in the 2000s BC.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Lynn, Commerce and Economic Change in West Africa (1997) Introduction pp.1–2 (PDF pp.21–22). The earlier archaeological claims (5,000–6,000 years; Egyptian trade) are cited there to notes not seen; compare fats-8000bc-1200bc::ec7 for the Abydos fat.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Wang Zhen’s oil press and the tallow-tree candle

entries.label: Candles from the Chinese tallow tree
entries.hint: The oil of the fruit of the Chinese tallow tree (Sapium sebiferum) is hard and can be poured to form candles, used everywhere in Guangnan; another tree’s oil, from the plant whose root is the drug wu yao, was used by villagers for torches, but its smoke smelled bad.
entries.note: SECONDARY (translation read in Needham): Needham, SCC 6.5 (2000) p.441 (PDF p.469), translating Chi le pien (see th1); Needham refers to SCC 6.1 pp.490–2, 498 for the plants.

entries.label: Wang Zhen describes the Chinese oil press
entries.hint: Wang Zhen’s Nong shu (1313) gives the first description of an oil press in Chinese literature, the ‘sleeping trough’ and ‘standing trough’: sesame is stir-fried, broken in a trip hammer or mill, steamed and bound with straw into round cakes, packed into a trough with wooden blocks and tightened with a wedge struck from above; oil runs into a vessel. Needham reads this as a wedge press, the type the Chinese had been using all along, and notes that the drawings do not match the text.
entries.note: SECONDARY (translation read in Needham): Needham, SCC 6.5 (2000) pp.441–443 (PDF pp.469–471), citing Nung shu ch.16 p.296 and the same passage in Nung cheng chhüan shu (1639); Needham also compares Greek and Roman presses (see fats-300bc-600ad::te1).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Spanish oil north, Egyptian linseed oil east

entries.label: Linseed oil from Egypt to Syria and Aden
entries.hint: Linseed oil was exported from Egypt to olive-growing Syria and to Aden in south Arabia, while olive oil, soap and wax came to Egypt from Tunisia and occasionally from Palestine and Syria; flax went from Egypt to Tunisia and Sicily. The Geniza merchants’ traffic shows two fat economies exchanging.
entries.note: ANCHOR (documents read): Goitein (1967) vol.1 pp.120 and 154 (PDF pp.156, 190). Span as for ec3.

entries.label: A Tunisian merchant in Palermo: five thousand dinars of oil, with Muslim and Jewish partners
entries.hint: In a Geniza letter of about 1064 a Tunisian merchant staying in Sicily writes that all his dealings in olive oil, which amounted to the enormous sum of five thousand dinars, were made not on his own account but in partnership with Muslims and Jews, inhabitants of Palermo; he refers twice more to his Muslim partners. Goitein takes it as one of the straight partnerships of the eleventh century, lasting years and not merely ephemeral.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Goitein, A Mediterranean Society vol. II (1971), the section on partnerships, PDF p.316. Compare ec2 for Tunisian oil shipped to Egypt.

entries.label: Spanish oil goes north, wool and hides go south
entries.hint: Within fourteenth-century Spain, olive oil was exported from south to north and wool and hides from north to south, a microcosm of greater Europe, where butter and lard were the fat of the north and oil of the south. Kiple places the Etruscans and Phoenicians as carriers of the olive into Italy and North Africa and Iberia, ending a Greek monopoly.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Kiple, Cambridge World History of Food (2000) II.E.1 p.378 (PDF p.415), citing Chandler 1950 and Trager 1995 (neither read); the fourteenth-century remark is unsourced there.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: A Muslim scholar on cake makers’ sesame oil

entries.label: A Fustat shopkeeper’s stock of 1104: linseed oil, olives and lemon juice
entries.hint: A Geniza partnership of January 1104 shows what a small retail shop held: the investor put in 9 dinars in cash and the partner goods of the same value, among them two jars of linseed oil, containers of olives, glass vessels of lemon juice and empty glass vessels, with scales and lead weights. Orders written on tiny pieces of vellum ask a shopkeeper to hand the bearer oil, soap, wood, vegetables, lemon and sugar.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Goitein, A Mediterranean Society I (1967) p.150–151 (PDF p.187; printed pages from the PDF offset). A ‘soap seller’ is listed beside a ‘soap maker’ in a charity list on PDF p.186, showing that the trade and the craft were distinct.

entries.label: Sesame oil sprayed from the mouth: a Muslim scholar on Jewish cake makers
entries.hint: A fourteenth-century Muslim scholar describes how Jewish cake makers used to squirt sesame oil on their cakes from their mouths and warns the faithful not to defile themselves with a liquid that had been in an unbeliever’s mouth — a snippet of the interfaith life of the cook-shop and of how oil moved through the Egyptian bazaar.
entries.note: SECONDARY (a hostile source): Goitein (1967) vol.1 p.114 (PDF p.150), quoting the scholar without a citation in the passage read. The practice described is reported by an opponent and not otherwise attested here.
